title: Satya Nadella Says AI Alignment Will Not Simply Fall Out of Scaling
excerpt: On the 20VC podcast, Microsoft's CEO said capabilities have scaled as he expected but alignment has not, and urged companies to treat models as insider threats wrapped in deterministic controls.
body:
• Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said on the 20VC podcast that he no longer believes AI alignment will emerge automatically as models become more capable.
  • He said scaling has worked as he expected on capabilities, but alignment — ensuring AI behaves in line with human values and goals — has not followed.
  • In an October 10 post on X, Nadella argued companies should treat AI models as insider threats and assume models are compromised.
  • On the same podcast, he said most token usage will become commodity usage and that Copilot already uses a lot of cheaper models.

Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella has abandoned a belief he held for years: that making artificial intelligence systems more powerful would, by itself, make them easier to align with human values. Asked on a new episode of the 20VC podcast what he had changed his mind about over the past year, Nadella told host Harry Stebbings that the assumption no longer holds, according to Business Insider reporting summarized by Pivot News and KuCoin.

"I used to always think that alignment would just fall out. I no longer believe that. I think this alignment thing may be a harder, different problem."

— Satya Nadella, CEO, Microsoft

Alignment, as Nadella defined it, means ensuring AI behaves in line with human values and goals. Scaling has played out as he expected, and model capabilities have kept improving. Alignment has not come along for the ride.

From scaling laws to a separate problem

In the podcast transcript, Nadella traced the earlier view to 2018 and 2019, when he shared the scaling-laws conviction associated with figures including Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, Ilya Sutskever, Greg Brockman and Elon Musk. The change, he said, is that capability growth and controllability have come apart: as models grow, even their designers cannot fully predict their behavior, according to the KuCoin summary of the Business Insider report.

https://x.com/JonhernandezIA/status/2115097044964536737

The remarks extend a warning Nadella posted on X on October 10. In that post, he argued companies should treat AI models as insider threats and assume they are compromised. "We need to surround non-deterministic models with strong, deterministic system design, human controls, and reliable operating procedures, and establish industry standards where existing ones are insufficient," he wrote, in the wording reported by Pivot News.

Not a lone voice

Nadella is not the only senior figure to separate capability from control. Pivot News noted that OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei have both warned about AI threats, and that a letter signed by more than 1,000 AI workers in July warned that capabilities could advance faster than people's ability to understand or control the systems.

The 20VC episode, released October 26, ranged beyond alignment. Its agenda included whether companies should assume every AI model is compromised, how to stop AI agents from causing harm, whether a model's chain of thought can be trusted, and whether China's lead in open-source AI is a safety risk.

Companies should own their intelligence

The same conversation carried a commercial argument that follows from the safety one. Nadella said most AI usage will become commodity usage. "I think predominantly token usage will be commodity token usage," he said, according to TIKR's account of the podcast, adding that there will always be a market for frontier models but that price competition will be intense among cheaper open-weight and closed models. Inside Copilot, he said, "we use a lot of closed source cheaper models."

That logic supports Microsoft's pitch that companies should keep their own data, evaluations and context separate from any single model, so models can be swapped as prices and quality change. If alignment also has to be engineered company by company — through system design, human oversight and operating procedures — then owning that control layer becomes part of the product, not an optional extra.

What it means, and what comes next

For Indian and Indian-American technology workers and founders, Nadella's remarks carry weight beyond one podcast: the Indian-American chief executive of Microsoft is arguing, in public, that the industry's next hard problem is not raw capability but control. Teams building on Copilot, Azure or any frontier model should expect more spending and scrutiny to shift toward evaluations, permissions, logging and human review around agents, rather than toward model access alone.

The test is whether Microsoft and its peers turn that framing into shared standards. Nadella's October 10 post called for industry standards where existing ones are insufficient. No standard was announced with the podcast. What has changed is the premise at the top of the industry's largest AI platform company: alignment is now described as a harder, different problem that has to be built, not a property that scale will deliver on its own.
